name: Equitable Holdings, Inc.

profile.description: Equitable Holdings is a New York-based retirement, protection and asset-management company founded in 1859 and known as AXA Equitable Holdings until January 2020 [4]. It operates Individual Retirement (variable and buffered annuities), Group Retirement (tax-advantaged plans for educators, municipalities and nonprofits), Investment Management and Research (AllianceBernstein), and Protection Solutions (life and group benefits) [4]. CEO Mark Pearson leads the company [2]. In Q3 2026 it reported non-GAAP operating earnings of $595M ($2.13/share, +19% YoY) and GAAP net income of $1.1B, with net inflows of $1.1B in Retirement, $2.7B in Wealth Management and $6.6B in Asset Management [1].

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): The most visible recent extension is wealth management. Wealth planning grew 12% in 2025, and Equitable closed the acquisition of Stifel Independent Advisors in Q1 2026, adding 110+ advisors and ~$9B of client assets [2]. These are incremental extensions of an advisor-distribution model rather than new products or a pivot. AI Deployment (0/2): Searches surfaced no AI products shipped to clients and no quantified AI-driven savings; a passing headline about AI coaching for client relationships had no detail [2]. Market Share (1/2): Equitable is a meaningful retirement and asset-management player, with Q3 2026 net inflows of $1.1B in Retirement, $2.7B in Wealth Management and $6.6B in Asset Management, but no share-leadership data was found [1]. Product Pipeline (0/2): No named next-generation products with launch timelines were identified. R&D Intensity (0/1): No R&D expense is reported [5].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Equitable frames its purpose around helping clients secure their financial well-being for retirement. That is clear about what it does and for whom, but it is not distinctive among retirement-focused insurers, and its 167-year history has not made the mission a differentiating force. Community Impact (0/2): Searches returned no evidence of quantified community or foundation programs; results were dominated by litigation over cost-of-insurance rate increases on 2004-2007 universal life policies and a variable-annuity volatility-management class action [3]. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention or tenure data was found. Insider Buying (0/2): FMP insider data shows net selling, with 20 insider sales and no open-market purchases in each of Q2 and Q3 2026, and 147K shares disposed against 49K acquired in Q3 [6].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on dividend metrics. Forward P/E of 6.1x scores 1.0 (yfinance) [4]. Payout ratio of 24.8% (FMP TTM) scores 1.0, and the 5-year dividend CAGR of 9.7% (annual dividends $0.66 in 2020 to $1.05 in 2025, derived from FMP dividend history) scores 1.0 at 2x weight [7]. Eight consecutive years of payments since the 2018 IPO score 0.8 at 2x weight, and 7 years of growth score 0.7 [7]. D/E of 586% scores 0.0 (shareholders' equity is very small and turns negative ex-noncontrolling interests on FMP's basis). ROE of -25.1% and revenue growth of -29.8% YoY also score 0.0; GAAP revenue swings with derivative and hedge marks [4][5]. The 5-year revenue CAGR of -1.2% (FY2020 $12.4B to FY2025 $11.7B) scores 0.25. Profit margin uses FMP's TTM bottom-line margin of 2.6%, which includes Q3 2026's $1.1B GAAP profit (yfinance's -8.7% predates it), and scores 0.13 [1][5]. Weighted sum 6.69 / 12 = 5.6, rounded to 6. Liquidity floor cleared at ~$154M daily dollar volume.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (6/9): Equitable's core earnings come from regulated annuity and life-insurance balance sheets and a captive advisor force, and AI cannot easily replicate state insurance licensing, long-duration guarantees or advisor-client trust. The company is leaning into advisor-led growth through the Stifel Independent Advisors deal and selective recruiting [2]. Exposure is higher in AllianceBernstein's active asset management and in commoditized advice, where AI-driven portfolio tools and lower-cost digital platforms could pressure fees. No analyst commentary specific to Equitable's AI exposure was found. AI Opportunity (0/1): Equitable discloses no AI-related revenue [2].

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, Equitable is a durable institution (founded 1859) whose current leadership speaks mainly in finite terms: operating EPS growth above 15%, capital-return targets and cash generation [1][2]. Its long life comes from the nature of insurance liabilities more than from a Just Cause that people sacrifice for. Long-running policyholder litigation over cost-of-insurance increases and volatility-management strategies suggests that, at times, balance-sheet protection has come before customer trust [3].

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): The purpose of helping clients secure financial well-being in retirement is service-oriented, but it reads as category marketing shared with every retirement provider. Management communication emphasizes earnings growth (operating EPS +22% year-to-date, exceeding the 15%+ 2026 target) and capital deployment rather than a vision that shapes strategic tradeoffs [1].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Leadership is stable under CEO Mark Pearson, and executives describe the Stifel advisors as a cultural fit with Equitable's own advisors, signaling some attention to culture during integration [2]. No employee-sentiment or retention data was found either way, so this scores as adequate.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No management commentary was found that acknowledges competitors' strengths or frames rivals as benchmarks for improvement; competitive messaging focuses on Equitable's own flows and earnings targets [1][2].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Equitable has shifted from an AXA-owned insurer to an independent company (renamed January 2020) and is expanding toward advisor-led wealth management, which grew 12% in 2025 and was extended by the Stifel acquisition [2][4]. These changes are incremental and build on existing distribution rather than abandoning a core business.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (0/2): Research found no example of leadership sacrificing near-term earnings for long-term capability. Capital allocation is framed around EPS growth targets and shareholder returns, and insiders have been consistent net sellers through 2025-2026 [1][6].

investment_thesis: Equitable trades at $54.26, or just 6.1x forward earnings, while Q3 2026 non-GAAP operating EPS rose 19% to $2.13 and year-to-date operating EPS is up 22%, above the 15%+ growth guided for 2026 [1][4]. TTM non-GAAP operating earnings reached $2.07B, with a non-GAAP operating ROE (ex-AOCI) of 39%. All three growth engines saw positive net flows in Q3: $1.1B in Retirement, $2.7B in Wealth Management and $6.6B in Asset Management [1]. The dividend is well covered at a 24.8% payout, and the quarterly rate has risen every year since the 2018 IPO, from $0.13 to $0.30 (9.7% 5-year CAGR) [7]. The Stifel Independent Advisors deal adds 110+ advisors and ~$9B of client assets to the higher-multiple wealth business [2].
thesis_continued: The bear case is earnings quality and balance-sheet opacity. GAAP results swing widely with hedging and derivative marks: FY2025 had a $1.44B net loss to common after $1.23B of profit in FY2024, revenue fell 29.8% YoY in the latest quarter, and the 5-year revenue CAGR is -1.2% [4][5]. Book equity is very thin or negative depending on the measure (D/E 586% on yfinance), which leaves little cushion if equity markets or interest rates move sharply against the variable-annuity book. Litigation over cost-of-insurance increases and volatility-management strategies has been ongoing for years [3]. For faith-aligned investors, the Inspire Impact Score of -49 (MISALIGNED, citing LGBT activism) is a significant negative.
key_catalysts: Delivering above 15% non-GAAP operating EPS growth for full-year 2026; year-to-date growth of 22% through Q3 sets up a beat [1]
Wealth Management scaling — $2.7B of Q3 net inflows plus Stifel Independent Advisors (~$9B in assets) shifting the mix toward capital-light, higher-multiple fee earnings [1][2]
Continued dividend growth — the quarterly dividend was raised to $0.30 in 2026, with only 24.8% of TTM earnings paid out [7]
key_risks: Market-sensitive GAAP earnings — hedge and derivative marks on the variable-annuity book drove a $1.44B FY2025 net loss to common despite positive operating earnings, and a sharp equity or rate move could repeat this [5]
Thin or negative book equity (D/E 586%) leaves little capital cushion and makes the company dependent on regulatory capital and reinsurance arrangements [4]

Policyholder litigation — class actions over cost-of-insurance increases on 2004-2007 universal life policies and the variable-annuity volatility-management strategy carry legal and reputational risk [3]
